title: Your Detailed Guide to Packshot Photography
summary: Packshot photography for e-commerce teams: marketplace specs, £ and € prices, how to brief a shoot, and how to scale without shipping stock to a studio.
body_markdown:
## Your shopper meets the photo before the product


Picture a shopper in Lyon scrolling a marketplace on her phone. Forty listings for the same kind of moisturizer flick past, and she stops on one. Not because of the copy or the price. She stops because the jar looks real: label sharp, cap the right shade of matte green, sitting on clean white like it's already on her shelf.


That jar is a packshot, and for most online catalogs it's the first thing a buyer judges. Eurostat's 2025 e-commerce survey found that 78% of EU internet users aged 16 to 74 had bought goods or services online in the past year. Get the image wrong and you pay twice: in lost clicks, and in returns when the product doesn't match the photo.


This guide is for the person who buys packshots, not the person who shoots them: the specs that decide whether images get accepted, what packshots cost per SKU in pounds and euros, how to brief a shoot and how to produce them at scale.


One product, one angle, nothing else in the frame. That restraint is what marketplaces ask for.


## What is packshot photography?


Packshot photography is product imagery shot to a fixed, repeatable standard: one product, a plain background (usually pure white), even lighting and nothing that distracts from the item. The Cambridge Business English Dictionary defines a packshot as a photograph or short piece of film showing a product and its package in a way that can be used to advertise it. You'll also see it written as pack shot or pack-shot, and teams in Germany, France and the Netherlands use "packshot" as-is.


## Packshot vs product photography: what's the difference?


Product photography is the umbrella term for any image made to show or sell a product. A packshot is one specific kind: the product isolated on a plain background, shot to the same standard as the rest of the range. Every packshot is product photography, but most product photography isn't a packshot.


• Packshots: the product alone on white or a neutral background, built for marketplace main images, listing grids and retailer data feeds where shoppers compare items.


• Lifestyle images: the product in use, in a real setting, built for desire and context.


• Flat lays: products arranged and shot from overhead. Our guide to[flat lay photography](https://www.snappr.com/blog/flat-lay-photography) covers the styling side.


The purpose changes how each is bought. A packshot brief is a specification (background, angles, crop, file size, naming) repeated across hundreds of SKUs, so it's planned and priced per product. A lifestyle brief is creative direction for a few hero images. For the wider picture, see[what product photography is and how it's used](https://www.snappr.com/blog/what-is-product-photography) .


## Why packshots carry so much weight


Salsify's 2026 Consumer Research, a survey of 2,712 shoppers in the U.S., U.K. and Canada, found that 61% consider product images and videos the most important product page element for completing a purchase, ahead of pricing and reviews.


Images cost you after the sale too. The same Salsify research found that 45% of shoppers had returned an online purchase in the past year because of incorrect product content, and its full report lists "images didn't match the product" as the first example. That's the expensive failure: a sale you paid to acquire, shipped, then refunded. Our breakdown of[product photos that sell](https://www.snappr.com/blog/product-photos-that-sell) goes deeper on the business case.


## The standard packshot set


A packshot isn't one photo. It's a set, and it should be identical for every SKU in a category so your listing grid looks like one brand rather than forty. The GS1 Product Image Standard (Release 5.1, September 2026), the global rulebook for product images shared between brands and retailers, recommends a center front view at 15 degrees of top elevation, with left and right 15-degree views when warranted. Most catalogs build from this list:


• Front hero (the main image)


• Left and right three-quarter views


• Back, including any ingredient panel or label


• Close-ups of texture, stitching or finish


• Group or multipack shot, where you sell bundles


360 packshot images are frames shot as the product rotates on a turntable, stitched so shoppers can drag to turn it. They suit footwear, electronics and eyewear, and they're usually the priciest item on the list, so commission them for top sellers first. Catalogue photography for apparel has its own rules: Amazon's main image guide for adult clothing requires a standing model and forbids a visible mannequin. Our guide to[apparel photography services](https://www.snappr.com/blog/apparel-photography-services) covers fashion at volume.


## Marketplace and retailer specs, side by side


Beautiful images still get rejected when the crop, size or background breaks a channel's rules. Check the specs before the shoot.


Amazon (UK, Germany, France):


• Background: Pure white, RGB 255, 255, 255, for the main image


• Size: Minimum 500 px on the longest side; 1,000 px or more enables zoom


• Framing and other rules: Product fills 85% of the image; whole product in frame; one unit only


Google Merchant Center:


• Background: A clean, unobstructed view of the product; no text, watermarks or promotional overlays


• Size: At least 500 x 500 px; 1,500 x 1,500 px or more recommended


• Framing and other rules: Product fills between 75% and 90% of the image


Zalando:


• Background: White primary packshots get a light gray background applied automatically


• Size: Minimum 762 x 1,100 px; best practice 1,801 x 2,600 px


• Framing and other rules: Portrait aspect ratio of 1:1.44; JPG in sRGB; maximum 20 MB


bol.com:


• Background: White, neutral background with no visible shadows for the main image


• Size: Minimum 500 x 500 px; zoom works from 1,200 x 1,200 px


• Framing and other rules: No models, text, or front, side and rear views combined in one image


GS1 Product Image Standard:


• Background: White (RGB 255, 255, 255) or transparent


• Size: Web images 900 x 900 to 2,400 x 2,400 px; high resolution from 2,401 x 2,401 px


• Framing and other rules: Subject centered to cover 95% of the canvas; clipping path recommended


Amazon's 85%, Google's 75% to 90% and GS1's 95% don't agree, so shoot with generous margins and crop per channel afterward. Zalando's tall 1:1.44 frame means leaving space above and below the product. And pure white means RGB 255, 255, 255: a soft gray that looks white on your monitor will fail.


## What packshot photography costs per SKU


Packshots sit in the e-commerce budget, and that budget is planned per SKU. Whatever a supplier quotes, the number that matters is what each product costs once it's live with its full image set.


The arithmetic: SKUs multiplied by angles per SKU gives the number of finished images. Two hundred SKUs with three views is 600 images. Colorways usually count as separate SKUs, since each needs its own main image, and adding one angle across a range multiplies the whole budget.


### Send-out studios: priced per image


Marszal Studio, based in Poland, lists a white-background packshot at €9 net per photo, or €18 net with premium retouching, on its pricing FAQ as of October 2026. At three angles that's €27 to €54 per SKU before shipping. Whito's August 2026 review of 40 published UK price lists puts white-background product shots at £10 to £25 an image at volume, or £30 to £75 per SKU at three angles.


### On-location: priced from your SKU list


Snappr works from your SKU count rather than a blind hourly quote. When you book, you enter the shoot style, product size, number of unique items and angles per item, and the booking returns a duration and a fixed price before you commit. Every photo is included, so colorways don't stack up per-image charges. Snappr's base prices for an all-inclusive shoot are £139 for one hour, £229 for two and £409 for four in the UK, and €99, €149 and €249 in Germany, France and the Netherlands, plus a 15% service fee at checkout. That's why its[product photographer page for Berlin](https://www.snappr.com/best-photographers/berlin-de/product) lists shoots from €114: the €99 base plus the fee.


To compare quotes fairly, divide each total, including shipping and retouching, by the number of products that come back with a complete, channel-ready image set. Reflective products, deep retouching and 360 spins all push the number up. Our[product photography pricing guide](https://www.snappr.com/blog/product-photography-pricing) compares the billing models in more detail.


## How to brief a packshot shoot


Every question a photographer has to ask mid-shoot is time you're paying for. Cover these five points in writing:


• Shot list by category. Group products by shape and finish (bottles, boxes, garments) and define the angle set for each group once, so similar products get batched under the same light.


• Background and files. Write "pure white, RGB 255, 255, 255", and ask for a clipping path on each image, as GS1 recommends, plus a high-resolution master and web exports per channel.


• Color accuracy. Send a physical sample of each colorway and ask for a gray card at the start of each light setup.


• Naming. Pick GTIN, internal SKU code or marketplace ID, plus a facing code per angle. Our piece on[catalog management](https://www.snappr.com/blog/catalog-management) covers how images fit a PIM or DAM.


• Product prep. Remove price stickers, steam garments and wipe packaging. GS1 also recommends removing batch details such as best-before dates from final images.


## Studio send-out vs on-location vs AI


Studio send-out means shipping products to a studio with a fixed set. Permanent coves and turntables are hard to beat for 360 spins and long runs of identical items. The tradeoff is logistics: Marszal Studio's FAQ lists packing and up to 10 days of free product storage as part of the service, which tells you how long stock can be away. For pre-launch samples or one-offs, that's a real cost.


On-location means a photographer comes to your office, warehouse or store with a portable white backdrop and lighting. Nothing gets boxed or couriered, your team pulls the next SKU off the shelf while the last one is on set, and you can add a few lifestyle frames in the same visit. It suits brands with stock across several sites and fast-moving ranges.


AI is good at clean-up around a real photo: removing a background, extending a canvas, fixing a crease. It's risky when it invents the product, because a slightly wrong label or color is exactly the mismatch that drives returns, and Zalando's image guidelines tell partners not to submit low-quality or unnatural AI-generated images. Photograph the real product, then let software handle backgrounds and crops. Our guide to[AI product photography](https://www.snappr.com/blog/ai-product-photography) covers where that line sits.


Bulky products like furniture make the strongest case for on-location packshots: nothing gets crated or couriered.


## Scaling packshots across a catalog


The hard part starts when a range grows to hundreds of SKUs, new products land monthly, and stock sits across a head office, warehouses and stores in several countries. That's the problem Snappr was built for: a vetted local photographer comes to wherever the products are and shoots to your brief, at a price fixed before you book. For ongoing programs, Snappr Enterprise adds:


• Centralized creative guidelines, so a photographer in Manchester and one in Munich deliver the same look.


• Central editing, with background removal and retouching handled before delivery.


• API-triggered shoots, so a photoshoot can start the moment a new product enters your systems.


• Reporting on every shoot across teams and sites.


Snappr's Enterprise page reports 339M+ photos captured worldwide.


## Get your catalog shot where it already lives


If your next launch means boxing up samples and waiting on a studio queue, there's another way.[Talk to Snappr's Enterprise team](https://www.snappr.com/enterprise) about on-location packshot photography across your sites, built to your marketplace specs.


## Frequently asked questions


### What is packshot photography?


Packshot photography is clean, standardized product photography, usually a single product on a pure white background with even lighting. It's used for e-commerce main images, product listing grids, catalogs and retailer data feeds, where every product needs to look consistent.


### What is the difference between a packshot and product photography?


A packshot is one type of product photography. Product photography also covers lifestyle images, flat lays and on-model shots, while a packshot isolates the product on a plain background so shoppers can compare it with other items.


### How much does packshot photography cost?


Plan it per SKU by multiplying your product count by the angles each one needs. Send-out studios charge per image: around €9 net per packshot at Marszal Studio, and £10 to £25 per image at volume across the UK price lists Whito reviewed. At three angles that works out to €27 to €54 per SKU, or £30 to £75 per SKU. Snappr prices on-location shoots from your number of products and angles per product, from a base price of £139 in the UK and €99 in Germany, France and the Netherlands, plus a 15% service fee at checkout.


### What background should a packshot have?


Pure white in most cases. Amazon requires RGB 255, 255, 255 for main images, and bol.com asks for a white, neutral background with no visible shadows. Ask for a clipping path as well, so you can switch to transparent or a channel-specific background later without reshooting.


### How many packshots do I need per product?


Plan on a main front image plus several supporting angles and details. Amazon's product image guide recommends at least six additional images and one video per listing, and the GS1 Product Image Standard recommends a front view plus left and right views where warranted.


### Can AI make packshots?


AI is useful for editing real product photos, such as removing backgrounds or resizing for different channels. Generating the product itself is riskier, since small errors in color or labels lead to returns, and Zalando's guidelines tell partners not to submit low-quality or unnatural AI-generated images.
